#702. NASA discovers Jupiter’s invisible shield is more complex than Earth’s

NASA's Juno spacecraft has uncovered remarkable new details about how Jupiter withstands the constant stream of high-energy particles flowing from the Sun. The findings reveal that the solar system's largest planet relies on a much more complex system of plasma waves and shock regions than Earth does.

Led by scientists at the University of Iowa, the research provides the most detailed observations yet of Jupiter's bow shock, an invisible boundary where particles from the Sun encounter the planet's magnetic environment. The discovery reveals important differences in how Jupiter and Earth respond to these incoming particles.

Beyond Jupiter, the results could also help scientists understand some of the most powerful events in the universe, including the extreme shock waves associated with exploding stars.

How Jupiter Protects Itself From the Solar Wind

The Sun continuously releases a stream of electrically charged particles called the solar wind. These particles travel through space at tremendous speeds, often faster than the speed at which sound waves move through the surrounding plasma. When the solar wind approaches a planet with a magnetic field, it encounters a boundary known as the bow shock.

At Earth, this boundary plays an important protective role. It slows and heats the incoming particles, helping redirect much of the solar wind around the planet. Without this process, more harmful particles could reach Earth's atmosphere, potentially making conditions less favorable for life.

Jupiter also has a bow shock, but its enormous size, powerful magnetic field, and gaseous composition make it a particularly interesting place to study how these boundaries behave. Scientists have long wanted to understand whether Jupiter handles the solar wind differently from Earth and what those differences might reveal about other objects throughout the universe.

Scientists Discover a More Complex Defense System

Using measurements from Juno, researchers discovered that Jupiter relies on plasma waves with multiple frequencies to slow and heat incoming solar particles. These different frequencies, known as "harmonics," create a more elaborate wave pattern than the one typically observed at Earth.

The process can be compared to music. Just as several notes played together produce a richer sound than a single note, plasma waves containing multiple frequencies can interact with incoming particles in more complex ways. This allows Jupiter's bow shock to transfer energy to more particles, heating them and reducing their speed.

Earth's bow shock, by comparison, primarily uses plasma waves concentrated around a single frequency. That simpler arrangement is generally sufficient for the conditions encountered near our planet.

"Jupiter has found its own way to deal with the solar wind, through plasma waves that are stronger and exhibit richer harmonic structures," says Jayasri Joseph, a postdoctoral researcher in the Department of Physics and Astronomy at Iowa and the study's corresponding author. "That's important because if you have multiple frequencies, you can heat more particles in the solar wind and slow them down."

The researchers identified another striking difference in how the two planets interact with the solar wind.

Before incoming particles reach Jupiter's main bow shock, they can encounter smaller shock structures called shocklets. These additional regions help slow the solar wind before it arrives at the primary shock boundary.

Earth's bow shock, in contrast, generally serves as the main region where the incoming solar wind is slowed and redirected. Jupiter's additional shock structures reveal a more complicated process for managing the energy carried by solar particles.

"Earth does not need to take these extra steps to handle the solar wind because the impact isn't as powerful," says Bill Kurth, a research scientist in Iowa's Department of Physics and Astronomy and a coauthor of the study.

Kurth has participated in NASA's Juno mission since the spacecraft launched in 2011.

What Jupiter Can Teach Us About Exploding Stars

Although these observations focus on Jupiter, their significance could extend far beyond our solar system.

Shock waves occur throughout the universe, particularly in environments where enormous amounts of energy are released. Some of the most extreme examples are found in supernova remnants, the expanding clouds of material left behind when certain dying stars explode.

These cosmic shock waves are vastly more powerful than those encountered near Jupiter. However, the physical processes that control how energy moves through plasma share important similarities. By examining Jupiter's bow shock in unprecedented detail, scientists can investigate mechanisms that would be much harder to measure directly around distant stars.

"Because even more powerful shocks occur around astrophysical objects such as supernova remnants, Jupiter's bow shock offers a nearby natural laboratory for exploring and for understanding how nature converts enormous amounts of flow energy into heat and energetic particles," Joseph says.

Understanding these processes could improve scientific models of how shock waves transfer energy, heat particles, and shape environments across the universe.

NASA's Juno Makes Unprecedented Measurements

The breakthrough was made possible by observations Juno collected in December 2024. The NASA spacecraft has been orbiting Jupiter since July 2016, providing researchers with an extraordinary opportunity to investigate the giant planet and its surrounding environment.

A key part of the discovery came from the Juno Waves instrument, which was designed and built by physicists at the University of Iowa. The instrument measures electric and magnetic wave activity, allowing scientists to study the behavior of plasma around Jupiter.

Earlier spacecraft had detected the presence of bow shocks at outer planets, but they lacked the measurements needed to reveal the detailed structure of the plasma waves involved. Juno's observations have now provided a much clearer picture of how these waves behave at Jupiter.

The findings were published online on July 31 in Nature Communications in a study titled "Plasma wave observations from Juno spacecraft at the Jovian bow shock."

Additional contributors from the University of Iowa included Allison Jaynes, an associate professor in the Department of Physics and Astronomy, along with Jeremy Faden and Chris Piker, who provide research support in the same department.

The international research team also included Lynn Wilson III of NASA Goddard Space Flight Center; John Connerney of NASA Goddard Space Flight Center and the Space Research Corporation; Frederic Allegrini of the Southwest Research Institute and the University of Texas-San Antonio; Rob Wilson of the University of Colorado-Boulder; Ali Sulaiman of the University of Minnesota; Scott Boltion and Robert Ebert of the Southwest Research Institute; and Barry Mauk of the Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory.

Materials provided by University of Iowa. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#701. Jane Fonda ‘Didn’t Dare Imagine’ Democrats’ Blue Tsunami: ‘We Have to Block What’s Bad and Fight For What’s Good’

Jane Fonda was giddy Thursday night at the Women in Film Honors gala in Beverly Hills.

“I’m so excited,” she told me while practically skipping down the red carpet.

The longtime political activist is riding the Election Day blue wave that helped the Democrats take control of the House of Representatives and the Senate. Related Stories Cate Blanchett-Backed Group and Collection of Hollywood Stars File Brief in New York Times-OpenAI Lawsuit: Hollywood Has ‘Proven Infrastructure’ to License Content Letterboxd in Negotiations to Be Acquired by New York Times Company

“I felt pretty optimistic, but I didn’t dare imagine that it would be this broad,” Fonda said. “I’m just so proud of American people, that they were paying attention and it wasn’t just about affordability. [James] Talarico’s acceptance speech was a masterpiece and in it he said, ‘We voted to love our neighbor.’”

She added, “I’m so excited with how many incredible women have been elected to high important offices.”

As for the Democrats’ next move, Fonda said, “We have to be very smart. We can’t return to the old neoliberalism. We have to take off our corporate hat, take off our donor hat, and start doing things that are going to help working people in this country, and we have to rule with love. We don’t rule yet, but we have to block what’s bad and fight for what’s good.”

She continued, “It’s not just about accountability and investigations because there’s so much corruption and criminality, but it also has to be about really putting power in the hands of working people and making life better for them.”

Fonda said she knows a lot of the candidates who won their elections. “I have a PAC and I’ve been traveling the country meeting them. These are different kinds of people,” she said. “People are just pissed. They don’t want crime. They don’t want chaos. They don’t want corruption.”

Fonda was on hand the gala to help honor Salma Hayek, who received the Jane Fonda Humanitarian Award.

#700. Einstein's equations may explain the universe without dark energy

Mathematicians are raising a major challenge to one of modern cosmology's most widely accepted explanations: the idea that dark energy is driving the accelerating expansion of the universe.

A study published in Proceedings of the Royal Society A presents mathematical findings that researchers at the University of California, Davis, say reveal a fundamental instability in the standard model of the expanding universe. Their calculations suggest that cosmic acceleration could emerge naturally from Einstein's equations, potentially eliminating the need to invoke mysterious dark energy.

The work challenges the Lambda-cold dark matter model, the leading framework scientists use to describe the universe's evolution since the Big Bang. The researchers reached their conclusions by studying the Einstein-Euler equations, which combine Einstein's theory of general relativity with equations describing how fluids behave. Together, these mathematical tools help scientists investigate everything from galaxies and black holes to the expansion of the cosmos.

A Hidden Instability in Our Model of the Universe

To explain the problem, Blake Temple, the study's corresponding author and a distinguished professor emeritus of mathematics at UC Davis, offered a simple comparison: a pencil balanced vertically on its tip.

"All the forces are in balance when a pencil is standing on end, so it is a 'solution of the equations,'" he said. "But it's unstable. Any breath of air and it falls away."

According to Temple, the team's mathematical analysis shows that Friedmann spacetimes, which form the foundation of conventional models of cosmic expansion, are unstable at both small and large scales in the context of the Big Bang. He described the standard solution as exceptionally unstable.

"Unstable solutions in physics and science are considered not physical," Temple said. "You'll never observe them in nature."

This instability could have far-reaching consequences. If the universe naturally evolves away from the behavior predicted by these conventional models, its accelerating expansion might not require a separate form of energy to explain it. Instead, Temple argues, the answer could already be contained within Einstein's original theory of gravity.

"The instability of all Friedmann spacetimes to accelerated expansion suggests a simpler, more natural explanation for the acceleration of the universe than dark energy," he said.

Why Scientists Believe Dark Energy Is Expanding the Universe

For nearly three decades, dark energy has been the leading explanation for one of astronomy's most puzzling discoveries: the universe is not simply expanding, but its expansion is accelerating.

The concept has roots in Einstein's groundbreaking 1915 theory of general relativity, which describes gravity as the curvature of space and time. Einstein originally believed the universe was static, neither expanding nor contracting. To make his equations compatible with that assumption, he introduced a mathematical term that counteracted gravity, calling it the "cosmological constant."

That assumption changed after Edwin Hubble discovered evidence in 1929 that the universe was expanding. Einstein famously referred to his introduction of the cosmological constant as his "biggest blunder," since his original equations without the additional term could have predicted an expanding universe.

The cosmological constant returned to prominence in the 1990s, when astronomers discovered that cosmic expansion was speeding up. It became closely associated with dark energy, the name given to the unknown component thought to be responsible for this acceleration.

Today's standard cosmological framework builds on the Friedmann universe, a mathematical description in which space expands while matter remains evenly distributed across the cosmos at any given moment. This assumption of large-scale uniformity plays a central role in how scientists reconstruct the universe's history.

But Temple and his collaborators began questioning whether the underlying mathematics could remain stable, prompting them to investigate other possible explanations for the observed acceleration.

Could Einstein's Equations Explain Cosmic Acceleration?

The researchers initially considered whether a massive shockwave might help explain the universe's expansion and the unexpected acceleration associated with it.

"Our first idea was that maybe the universe was expanding because there was a shockwave, and the anomalous acceleration was the expanding wave behind that shockwave," Temple said. "Then we realized there's a family of self-similar solutions during the radiation epoch of the Big Bang, which might model that expanding wave."

In mathematics and physics, self-similar solutions describe patterns that retain their underlying structure when viewed at different scales. A familiar example is a fractal, in which similar shapes can appear at increasingly larger or smaller sizes.

The researchers identified a family of these solutions associated with the radiation-dominated period of the early universe, when radiation played a major role in determining how the cosmos evolved.

Building on their earlier work, they used a self-similar form of Einstein's equations to represent the standard cosmological model as a rest point, a mathematical state in which the system's defining variables remain unchanged. This approach allowed them to examine whether small departures from that state would disappear or grow over time.

Their analysis provided a mathematical framework for evaluating the stability of the standard model and, more broadly, Friedmann spacetimes during the matter-dominated era of the early universe, when matter became more influential than radiation.

A Mathematical Challenge to the Standard Big Bang Model

The results suggest that the conventional mathematical descriptions of the expanding universe are vulnerable to disturbances that grow rather than fade.

"We prove that, like Einstein's static model, the Friedmann spacetimes are all unstable to radial perturbation at large length scales," Temple said. "This appears to rule out the Lambda-cold dark matter model as a viable stable solution of the Einstein equations of general relativity, with or without dark energy."

Radial perturbations are disturbances that change with distance from a central point. In the researchers' mathematical framework, such changes can cause the behavior of an expanding universe to depart from the predictions of the standard Friedmann model.

"This means," he added, "that the Big Bang should generically look exactly like a Friedmann spacetime near the center of symmetry, but generically one should observe accelerations away from Friedmann far from the center."

In other words, the universe could behave much like the standard model predicts near a central region while exhibiting different expansion behavior farther away.

The researchers argue that this instability may offer a natural route to accelerated cosmic expansion without adding a cosmological constant or invoking dark energy. Their calculations indicate that the acceleration can emerge directly from the Einstein-Euler equations themselves.

The findings represent a theoretical challenge to standard cosmology rather than observational proof that dark energy is unnecessary. Establishing whether this alternative can describe the actual universe would require determining how well its predictions match astronomical observations.

Does the Universe Have a Special Location?

Beyond the dark energy question, the study also raises a more fundamental issue involving the Copernican principle.

Named after astronomer Nicolaus Copernicus, who helped overturn the belief that Earth sits at the center of the solar system, the principle holds that our location in the universe is not fundamentally special or privileged.

This assumption has become an important part of modern cosmology, supporting the view that the universe looks broadly similar when observed from different locations on sufficiently large scales.

The researchers' alternative mathematical framework introduces a center of spherical symmetry, raising questions about where an observer would need to be located for the model to agree with observations.

Temple argues that the Copernican principle must be applied consistently when evaluating competing explanations of the universe.

"Both the Lambda-cold dark matter model and a spherically symmetric spacetime produce a special place where we must lie for the model to be physically plausible," Temple said. "If this principle rules out one, it has to rule out the other."

The work opens another avenue for investigating why the universe's expansion is accelerating. Although dark energy remains a central component of the prevailing cosmological model, the researchers contend that the mathematics of general relativity may offer a different explanation for the same phenomenon.

If further theoretical and observational work supports their interpretation, it could lead to a significant reassessment of how scientists understand cosmic expansion and the mathematical foundations of the Big Bang.

The research received funding from the United Kingdom's Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council and the American Institute of Mathematics SQuaREs Program.

Materials provided by University of California - Davis. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#699. FedEx beats expectations, raises outlook in first report since calendar adjustment

FedEx on Wednesday reported quarterly earnings that beat Wall Street expectations on the top and bottom lines and raised its full-year outlook for its newly realigned fiscal year.

Shares of the company fell slightly in extended trading.

Here's how the company performed for the period ended Sept. 30 compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:

The company reported net income for the quarter of $290 million, or $1.21 per share, compared with $650 million, or $2.73 per share, during the comparable period a year prior. Adjusting for one-time items — including losses related to short-term investments, gains on the extinguishment of debt and certain restructuring costs — FedEx reported adjusted earnings per share of $3.74.

It marks the first report of FedEx's realigned fiscal year, moving the end of its calendar from May 31 to Dec. 31. The report also comes after the company successfully spun out FedEx Freight into a separate publicly traded company.

FedEx said its express U.S. segment operating income increased in the quarter, primarily driven by higher package yields and volume.

"As our strong operating results and adjusted free cash flow demonstrate, FedEx is winning across high-value market segments while we optimize our network, driving an increase to our full-year outlook," CEO Raj Subramaniam said in a statement.

For the full year, the company is now expecting adjusted earnings per share of between $18 and $18.60, compared with a prior range of $16.90 to $18.10. FedEx also said it's revising its 2026 revenue growth expectation to a roughly 12% year-over-year increase, up from previous guidance of an 11% increase.

Earlier this week, FedEx named former AutoZone executive Jamere Jackson as the company's new chief financial officer, effective Nov. 30. He replaces Claude Russ, who served as the interim CFO since June 1. John Dietrich was announced as stepping down from that role in April.

#698. IIHF ordered to allow Russia back into world championships

The Court of Arbitration for Sport has ruled that Russian teams must be allowed to take part in international ice hockey tournaments. The IIHF had banned Russia following the country's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

In a statement published on Friday, the Court of Arbitration for Sport(CAS) said it had overturned International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) decisions, which exclude Russia from events during the 2026-27 season, including the men's and women's world championships.

In the statement, the CAS cited a lack of sufficient evidence to support security concerns cited by the IIHF in its decisions to exclude Russian teams from competition.

Specifically, it ordered the IIHF to allow Russia to participate in five upcoming tournaments, including the Men's Ice Hockey World Championship in Germany next May and the Women's Ice Hockey World Championship scheduled for November 2027 in Canada.

The first tournament affected by the ruling is the Men's World Junior Championship, which opens in Edmonton on December 26. The Women's World Championship being hosted by Denmark starting next Friday, November 6, is not mentioned in the statement.

Russian Sports Minister Mikhail Degtyaryov hailed the CAS ruling, writing on the Telegram social media app that CAS had "recognized the demands of the Russian Hockey Federation on key points as justified."

The IIHF expressed disappointment with the ruling , saying it "maintains that its decisions were necessary to protect the safety and security of all participants and safeguard the integrity of its competitions."

"While the IIHF respects the authority of CAS and will act in accordance with its ruling, the outcome does not remove the concerns that informed its assessments."

Germany's ice hockey association, the DEB, also expressed disappointment at the decision.

"Our position is unchanged: We reject the return of Russian national teams to international ice hockey tournaments," said DEB chairman Frank Lutz, who added that the ruling had fundamentally changed things for Germany as hosts of the 2027 Men's World Championship.

"Allowing Russia to participate entails significant security-related, political, and economic consequences for us as hosts. We are now evaluating the ruling together with the IIHF and will provide information regarding the next steps."

In its statement, the IIHF also pointed to "significant practical implications for competitions already at an advanced stage of preparation," which includes the men's tournament to be hosted by Düsseldorf, Mannheim and Gelsenkirchen and for which the groups have already been drawn.

Among the teams slated to participate in the tournament are Ukraine, who are set to make their return to ice hockey's international top flight after winning promotion at this year's Division 1 tournament in Poland. Ukraine had spent two decades in international ice hockey's second tier since being relegated in 2007.

Unsurprisingly, the Ukranian federation (FHU) has also condemned the CAS decision.

"The Ice Hockey Federation of Ukraine respects the authority and status of the CAS. At the same time, we express our deep indignation at this decision, made amidst a full-scale war," it said in a statement.

"The threats that served as the basis for the suspension of Russian teams in 2022 have not disappeared; on the contrary, they have only intensified."

The IIHF has barred Russian teams from its tournaments since shortly after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. This meant Russia also missed this year's prestigious Olympic hockey tournaments in Milan earlier this year.

Russia and its predecessor, the Soviet Union, are one of the most successful ice hockey-playing nations, having won 27 men's World Championships, second only to Canada (28).

Friday's ruling comes with the IIHF having just elected a new president – Germany's Franz Reindl took over from Luc Tardif of France earlier this month.

#697. Six popular sugar substitutes linked to faster brain aging

Sugar substitutes are often promoted as a healthier way to enjoy sweet foods and drinks without consuming as much sugar. However, new research suggests that some of these widely used sweeteners may have an unexpected downside for long-term brain health.

A study published in Neurology, the medical journal of the American Academy of Neurology, found that people who consumed the most low- and no-calorie sweeteners experienced significantly faster declines in memory and thinking skills than those who consumed the least. The association was particularly pronounced among people with diabetes.

Researchers examined seven sweeteners commonly used in foods and beverages: aspartame, saccharin, acesulfame-K, erythritol, xylitol, sorbitol and tagatose. These ingredients frequently appear in ultra-processed products, including diet sodas, flavored waters, energy drinks, yogurt and low-calorie desserts. Some are also sold separately for sweetening foods and beverages.

"Low- and no-calorie sweeteners are often seen as a healthy alternative to sugar; however, our findings suggest certain sweeteners may have negative effects on brain health over time," said study author Claudia Kimie Suemoto, MD, PhD, of the University of São Paulo in Brazil.

Importantly, the findings show an association rather than a proven cause-and-effect relationship. Researchers cannot conclude from this study that consuming these sweeteners directly damages the brain or causes memory loss.

Study Tracks Nearly 13,000 Adults for Eight Years

To investigate whether sugar substitutes might be connected to cognitive health, researchers analyzed data from 12,772 adults across Brazil. Participants were 52 years old on average when the study began and were followed for approximately eight years.

At the beginning of the study, participants completed detailed dietary questionnaires describing the foods and drinks they had consumed during the previous year. Researchers used these responses to estimate each person's daily intake of the seven sweeteners.

Participants were then separated into three groups according to how much of the sweeteners they consumed. Those in the lowest consumption group averaged 20 milligrams per day (mg/day), while those in the highest group averaged 191 mg/day. For comparison, 191 milligrams of aspartame is roughly the amount found in one can of diet soda.

Of the seven sweeteners examined, sorbitol had the highest average intake, at 64 mg/day. Sorbitol belongs to a category of sweeteners called sugar alcohols, which provide sweetness and are commonly used as sugar substitutes.

Throughout the study, participants completed cognitive assessments at three points: the beginning, middle, and end. These tests measured several abilities essential for everyday mental functioning, including memory, language, and the speed at which the brain processes information.

Researchers evaluated verbal fluency, or the ability to quickly retrieve and produce words, along with working memory, which allows people to temporarily hold and use information. They also tested word recall and processing speed to determine how these abilities changed over time.

High Sweetener Consumption Linked to 62% Faster Cognitive Decline

The results revealed a striking difference between people who consumed the most sweeteners and those who consumed the least.

After accounting for factors that could influence cognitive health, including age, sex, high blood pressure, and cardiovascular disease, researchers found that participants in the highest consumption group experienced a 62% faster decline in overall thinking and memory abilities compared with those in the lowest group.

That difference was equivalent to approximately 1.6 additional years of cognitive aging over the study period.

Even moderate consumption was associated with measurable differences. Participants in the middle group experienced a 35% faster decline than those consuming the least, equivalent to roughly 1.3 additional years of cognitive aging.

These estimates describe changes in cognitive test performance rather than a direct measurement of biological brain aging. They also do not mean that everyone who consumes artificial sweeteners will experience memory problems.

Stronger Links Found in Adults Under 60 and People With Diabetes

When researchers examined different age groups, they discovered that the association was not consistent across all participants.

Among adults younger than 60, higher sweetener consumption was linked to faster declines in verbal fluency and overall cognitive performance. However, researchers did not find a similar association among participants older than 60.

The relationship was also stronger in people with diabetes than in those without the condition. This finding is especially relevant because people with diabetes frequently turn to sugar substitutes to help manage their sugar intake.

Examining the sweeteners individually revealed another important distinction. Six of the seven substances were associated with faster declines in overall cognitive performance, particularly memory.

Those six were aspartame, saccharin, acesulfame-K, erythritol, sorbitol and xylitol.

Tagatose was the exception. Researchers found no association between its consumption and cognitive decline in this study. However, that finding does not establish that tagatose protects the brain or is necessarily safer than other sweeteners.

Should People Rethink Artificial Sweeteners?

The findings raise important questions about whether replacing sugar with low-calorie alternatives always delivers the health benefits consumers expect, particularly when it comes to the brain.

"While we found links to cognitive decline for middle-aged people both with and without diabetes, people with diabetes are more likely to use artificial sweeteners as sugar substitutes," Suemoto said. "More research is needed to confirm our findings and to investigate if other refined sugar alternatives, such as applesauce, honey, maple syrup or coconut sugar, may be effective alternatives."

Researchers also acknowledged several limitations. The analysis did not cover every artificial sweetener available on the market, so the findings cannot necessarily be applied to all sugar substitutes.

In addition, dietary information came from participants' own recollections of what they had eaten and drunk. Because people may forget foods, underestimate portions, or inaccurately report their habits, these estimates may not perfectly reflect actual sweetener consumption.

The observational design also means that other factors could help explain the relationship between sweetener intake and cognitive decline, despite researchers' efforts to account for several important health differences.

Further studies will be needed to determine whether the sweeteners themselves contribute to changes in brain function, why certain groups appear more strongly affected, and whether different sugar alternatives produce different long-term outcomes.

The research was supported by the Brazilian Ministry of Health, the Ministry of Science, Technology, and Innovation, and the National Council for Scientific and Technological Development.

Materials provided by American Academy of Neurology. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#696. Physicists created a tiny universe and watched time emerge without a clock

What if time is not a fundamental part of the universe, but something that emerges from the changes taking place inside it? A physicist at the University of Birmingham has created a miniature universe in the laboratory that offers a surprising new way to investigate this possibility.

Using thousands of atoms cooled to temperatures barely above absolute zero, Professor Giovanni Barontini demonstrated that the passage of time can be measured without relying on an external clock. Instead, a form of time emerges naturally from the behavior of particles within the experimental system.

The findings, published in Physical Review Research, provide experimental evidence for an intriguing idea in theoretical physics: Time may not be an essential ingredient of reality. It could arise from the relationships and changes occurring within the universe itself.

Why Some Physicists Think Time May Not Be Fundamental

We usually think of time as something that continuously moves forward, regardless of what happens around us. Seconds pass, planets orbit stars, and the universe evolves. But some theories of physics suggest that time may work very differently at the most fundamental level.

One example is the Wheeler-DeWitt equation, which appears in attempts to combine quantum mechanics with gravity. In this framework, the universe can be described as a single, unchanging quantum state, with no external clock marking the passage of time. Quantum particles can exhibit both wave-like and particle-like properties, but the universe as a whole does not necessarily have a built-in time variable.

This creates a major puzzle. If the universe has no external clock, how can anything happen in a particular order? What determines which events come first and which happen later?

One possibility is that time emerges from the changing relationships between different parts of the universe. Barontini designed an experiment to investigate whether such a process could be observed in the laboratory.

Creating a Miniature Universe With 24,000 Atoms

To build his miniature cosmos, Barontini used a cloud of approximately 24,000 atoms cooled to just a few billionths of a degree above absolute zero. At these extraordinarily low temperatures, quantum effects become especially important, allowing researchers to study behaviors that are normally difficult to observe.

The atoms were confined inside a carefully controlled quantum system designed to remain isolated from its surroundings. Two laser beams operating at different frequencies created a thin barrier that divided the system into two regions: an observed ('bright') region and an unobserved ('dark') region.

Although the overall system was isolated from the outside world, atoms could move between these two regions.

The bright region underwent repeated cycles of expansion and contraction, resembling simplified versions of two dramatic cosmological events. The expansion was analogous to the Big Bang, while the contraction resembled a Big Crunch, a hypothetical fate of the universe in which cosmic expansion eventually reverses and everything collapses inward.

The experiment did not recreate these actual cosmic events. Instead, it provided a simplified quantum model in which researchers could investigate how a sequence of events might be reconstructed without referring to a clock outside the system.

The key to the experiment was entropy, a concept in physics associated with the spread or disorder (entropy) of particles and energy.

Rather than using seconds or minutes, Barontini developed a way to track time through changes in how atoms were distributed within the miniature universe.

As atoms moved between the bright and dark regions, the distribution of particles in the bright region changed. These changes provided a way to define the system's progression through time, even when the bright region alternated between expansion and contraction.

When the particle distribution increased or decreased in its spread, the system continued moving forward according to this internal measure of time. When the distribution remained unchanged, the progression of this particular form of time effectively stopped.

Importantly, this did not mean that time literally stopped in the laboratory. It meant that the internal measure of time ceased advancing when the relevant changes in the system disappeared.

Barontini called this concept "entropic time." The experiment showed that this form of time has several important properties. It moves consistently in one direction, establishing what physicists call the "arrow of time," the distinction between past and future. It also places events in the correct sequence, even as the miniature universe expands and contracts.

Perhaps most surprisingly, entropic time does not always advance at the same rate. Its progression can speed up or slow down depending on how entropy changes within the system.

A New Clue to One of Physics' Biggest Mysteries

Professor Barontini said: "In some theories of the universe, especially quantum gravity, time doesn't appear as a built-in feature. Yet in everyday life, time flows from past to future -- why is this so, when most basic laws of physics work the same way forwards and backwards?

"This study provides the first controlled experimental evidence that 'time' can be defined by changes within a system rather than as the external 'ticking clock' we think of as time. It offers new insight into the nature of time in quantum gravity that could be used to describe dynamics just as effectively as conventional time."

The distinction between everyday time and the underlying laws of physics is especially important. Many fundamental physical equations work equally well whether time is mathematically reversed or allowed to move forward. Yet our experience of the world has a clear direction: We remember the past, not the future, and events unfold in a recognizable sequence.

Entropy has long played a central role in explaining this difference. Barontini's experiment takes that connection further by demonstrating how changes in entropy can provide an operational measure of time inside a controlled quantum system.

The findings also go beyond simply arranging events in the correct order.

Barontini demonstrated that a version of the Schrödinger equation, one of the foundational equations of quantum mechanics (Schrödinger), can be expressed using entropic time. This equation describes how the quantum state of a system evolves, including changes in the probability of finding particles in particular locations or states.

In other words, the internally generated measure of time could still be used to make predictions about the quantum system's behavior, much as conventional time is used in standard quantum mechanics.

Could a Tiny Universe Help Explain the Big Bang?

For decades, questions about the origin and fundamental nature of time have largely belonged to theoretical physics, particularly quantum cosmology and quantum gravity. These fields attempt to understand how the universe behaves when quantum effects and gravity must be considered together, including under the extreme conditions associated with the early cosmos.

Barontini's experiment offers a way to investigate some of these ideas using physical systems that scientists can create, manipulate, and observe.

The miniature universe continued to obey the established equations of quantum physics while providing a different way to describe its evolution. That makes it a potentially valuable testing ground for theories in which time is not assumed to exist independently of the system being studied.

Future experiments could extend this approach to more complicated quantum systems, allowing researchers to explore models of the Big Bang and the Big Crunch in greater detail. Similar techniques might eventually help simulate aspects of black holes or distinguish between competing explanations of how time emerges.

The experiment does not establish that time is an illusion or prove that our universe lacks fundamental time. Instead, it demonstrates something that was previously difficult to test: A quantum system can possess a meaningful internal measure of time without depending on an external clock.

By creating a miniature universe from just 24,000 atoms, researchers have gained a new experimental tool for investigating a question that has challenged physicists and philosophers for centuries: What makes time flow?

#695. Toothbrush zaps bacteria with electricity made when bristles move

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

The history of the manual toothbrush has been traced back to the Tang Dynasty in China. Credit: Valentyna Yeltsova/Getty

Researchers at Peking University in Beijing have developed a battery-less brush that destroys bacteria by generating its own electrical charge, rather than relying on mechanical friction alone. The work was published in Science Advances on 4 November1.

Generating electricity from brushing is a “new twist on an old concept,” says Frank Scannapieco, a periodontist and microbiologist at the University of Buffalo in New York. It might reduce plaque more efficiently, although more tests are needed to prove efficacy and safety, he says.

The researchers showed that the novel brush did not damage the tooth surface and was not toxic to human cells, but they did not look at long term safety or cost.

Bristled brushes — some form of which humans have used to clean teeth since the 10th century CE — primarily rely on motion to manually disrupt plaque, the films of saliva around teeth in which communities of bacteria grow.

The researchers made the bristles from polyvinylidene fluoride, a polymer which they stretched and heated to obtain its piezoelectric form — meaning it generates a charge when deformed.

When used to scrub teeth, the bending bristles release charges that create highly reactive forms of oxygen in nearby saliva. These damage bacteria cell membranes, say the researchers. When the bristles relax, the material reabsorbs the charges.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03586-y

Lu, Y. et al. Sci. Adv. 12, eaeg5744 (2026).

#694. Germany takes cautious approach on Israeli election results

German politicians have been slow to respond as they wait to see who is likely to comprise the next coalition. Many are also hoping for a government without religious hardliners.

Though it has been two days since Israel's parliamentary elections, German politicians are still being cautious to respond, as it is still unclear who will lead Israel's new government.

Although the right-wing bloc, including religious hardliners, led by incumbent Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is ahead of the opposition bloc led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, neither has a clear path to a governing majority in the Knesset.

Forming a coalition government is likely to be extremely difficult.

Martin Giese, spokesperson for German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul, declined to comment at Wednesday's regular government press conference in Berlin.

But he did stress that Germany has been in contact with numerous officials and politicians in Israel via Germany's ambassador. "The Jewish state and Germany are inextricably linked by our history, and we will do everything we can to work well with any future government," Wadephul said.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

One concern for the German government is providing aid to the people in Gaza, and protracted coalition negotiations could delay necessary progress.

"Winter is coming, and it will be difficult," Development Minister Reem Alabali Radovan, currently visiting Lebanon, warned in an interview with Politico. She underlined that there must be more opportunities for aid organizations to provide crucial assistance in Gaza and that it cannot wait for coalition negotiations.

In interviews with DW and broadcaster RTL, she spoke about the recent increase in attacks by Israeli settlers on Palestinians in the occupied West Bank and East Jerusalem.

"The radical settler violence must be stopped. The Netanyahu government remains in office on an interim basis, and this means that this situation must still be brought to an end," she said.

All settlement activity in the occupied Palestinian territories is considered illegal under international law.

Relations between Germany and Israel are traditionally close, in part because of Germany's historical responsibility for Nazi Germany's murder of millions of Jews during the Holocaust.

Recently, however, the German government has distanced itself from Netanyahu's policies, at least in its public rhetoric.

Most recently, Wadephul said after a major Israeli military operation near the city of Hebron: "Under international law, Israel is quite clearly obligated to uphold and protect the rights of Palestinians as well." Around 3,000 Palestinians were driven from their homes during the operation, which followed the reported killing of two Israeli soldiers by Palestinians.

In Berlin, there has long been speculation about whether Germany's policy toward Israel might change after Israel's 2026 election.

So far, one thing is clear: Unlike numerous other countries, including some in Europe, Germany does not intend to recognize a Palestinian state for the time being.

At the same time, Germany hopes that the future government will no longer include religious extremists, and in some cases far-right, politicians such as the current Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich.

"I think it would be best for Israel to form a government that is closer to the center of the political spectrum," Jürgen Hardt, foreign policy expert for the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) in the Bundestag, told DW. "Of course, that's something the people, and above all the elected politicians, will have to figure out. But it's encouraging that so many people participated in the election."

The Arab-majority parties led by Palestinian citizens of Israel made large gains in this election. They are usually classified as part of the current opposition camp. The historic results by these parties could lead them to play a kingmaker role in coalition formation.

However, Netanyahu’s bloc have ruled out working with the Arab-majority parties.

Eisenkot's opposition bloc has not yet said whether it would be willing to form such a coalition, but one of the Arab-majority parties, United Arab List/Ra'am, featured a Jewish candidate, and has stated its willingness to work with Eisenkot’s bloc to unseat Netanyahu.

Hardt believes a minority government led by Eisenkot and supported by parties representing Arab Israelis is conceivable.

"The major campaign carried out by Netanyahu's camp, aimed primarily against Arab Israelis, greatly mobilized the opposition, to the point where his camp no longer has a majority."

The vice president of the German Bundestag, Green Party politician Omid Nouripour, told DW: "Frankly, after all the turmoil that has occurred — for example, regarding judicial reform — this is good news for Israeli democracy."

This article was originally published in German.

#693. A surprising vitamin A discovery is changing what scientists know about vision

Scientists at Johns Hopkins University have uncovered a surprising role for a vitamin A derivative in the development of human vision. Their research reveals how this molecule works alongside thyroid hormones to help form the part of the eye responsible for our sharpest sight, challenging a scientific explanation that has stood for roughly 30 years.

The discovery centers on an unexpected transformation that occurs in the developing retina before birth. Certain cells that initially detect blue light appear to change into cells sensitive to red and green light, helping create the specialized arrangement needed for clear central vision.

Published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, the findings could reshape scientists' understanding of how human eyes develop. They may also help advance research into future treatments for macular degeneration, glaucoma, and other conditions that cause vision loss.

"This is a key step toward understanding the inner workings of the center of the retina, a critical part of the eye and the first to fail in people with macular degeneration," said Robert J. Johnston Jr., an associate professor of biology at Johns Hopkins University who led the study. "By better understanding this region and developing organoids that mimic its function, we hope to one day grow and transplant these tissues to restore vision."

How Scientists Recreated the Developing Human Retina

To investigate how human vision forms, Johnston and his colleagues turned to an innovative laboratory technique they have helped develop over the past several years. Instead of relying entirely on animal experiments, they grew miniature versions of human retinal tissue called organoids.

These small clusters of cells, grown from fetal cells, reproduce important features of developing human tissue. By observing the retinal organoids over several months, the scientists could follow changes that would otherwise be extremely difficult to study during pregnancy.

Their attention focused on the foveola, a tiny region at the very center of the retina. The retina is the light-sensitive layer at the back of the eye that converts incoming light into signals the brain can interpret. Within it, the foveola plays an especially important role in detailed central vision, which allows people to read, recognize faces, and distinguish fine details.

Although the foveola occupies only a small fraction of the retina, it is involved in approximately 50% of human visual perception, according to the researchers.

The Surprising Secret Behind Sharp Human Vision

One of the keys to understanding the foveola is a group of specialized light-detecting cells called cones. Unlike rod cells, which are particularly important for seeing in dim light, cones support daytime vision and allow us to perceive color.

Humans have three types of cone cells, each most sensitive to different wavelengths of light. These are commonly described as blue, green, and red cones. By comparing signals from these different cells, the brain can distinguish a remarkably broad range of colors.

However, the cones are not distributed evenly throughout the retina. The foveola contains red and green cones but lacks blue cones, which are found in other retinal regions. This precise arrangement is essential for the exceptionally sharp vision produced by the center of the eye.

For decades, researchers have struggled to explain how this pattern develops. One major obstacle is that commonly studied animals, including mice and fish, do not share the same retinal organization found in humans. That makes it difficult to use traditional animal models to investigate how these specialized cells develop.

The laboratory-grown human retinas offered a new opportunity to solve this longstanding mystery.

Vitamin A and Thyroid Hormones Trigger a Remarkable Change

The researchers discovered evidence that the arrangement of cones in the foveola develops through two coordinated processes. Together, they determine which types of cells form in the central retina and how some of those cells change as development continues.

During weeks 10 through 12 of fetal development, a small number of blue cones are initially present in the foveola. By week 14, however, these cells appear to have transformed into red and green cones.

The team identified two important chemical influences behind this process.

The first involves retinoic acid, a molecule produced from vitamin A. Retinoic acid helps regulate how cells develop and specialize throughout the body. In the developing retina, the breakdown of this molecule limits the formation of blue cones in the central region.

The second influence comes from thyroid hormones, which are best known for regulating metabolism but also have crucial roles in growth and development. In this case, the hormones appear to encourage the remaining blue cones to change into red and green cones.

"First, retinoic acid helps set the pattern. Then, thyroid hormone plays a role in converting the leftover cells," Johnston said. "That's very important because if you have those blue cones in there, you don't see as well."

Importantly, the discovery concerns how vitamin A signaling helps guide eye development before birth. It does not establish that taking vitamin A supplements can improve sharp vision in adults.

A Discovery That Challenges a 30-Year-Old Theory

The results offer a striking alternative to an explanation that has influenced vision research for decades.

Under the longstanding model, blue cones that initially appear in the foveola were thought to move away as the retina developed. Scientists generally assumed that once these cells became a particular type of cone, their identities remained fixed.

The new findings suggest something different. Rather than simply relocating, at least some blue cones may undergo a change in identity, becoming red or green cones as the eye develops.

"The main model in the field from about 30 years ago was that somehow the few blue cones you get in that region just move out of the way, that these cells decide what they're going to be, and they remain this type of cell forever," Johnston said. "We can't really rule that out yet, but our data supports a different model. These cells actually convert over time, which is really surprising."

The researchers have not completely ruled out the possibility that some cells migrate. Nevertheless, their observations support the idea that developing cone cells have more flexibility than previously recognized.

That possibility could fundamentally change how scientists study the formation of human color vision and the development of the retina's most specialized regions.

Could the Discovery Help Scientists Restore Lost Vision?

Beyond explaining how healthy eyes develop, the findings could have important implications for treating diseases that damage the retina.

One particularly promising application involves macular degeneration, a major cause of central vision loss, especially among older adults. The disease damages the macula, the retinal region responsible for detailed central vision, and can severely interfere with reading, driving, and recognizing faces. Although treatments can slow or manage certain forms of the disease, there is currently no cure.

Understanding how the retina creates its specialized light-sensitive cells could eventually help scientists produce healthy replacements in the laboratory.

Johnston's team is now working to improve its retinal organoids so they more closely reproduce the structure and function of the human eye. The long-term goal is to develop precisely controlled populations of photoreceptors, the cells that detect light, for potential transplantation into damaged retinas.

Katarzyna Hussey, a study author and former doctoral student in Johnston's laboratory, believes this approach could open an important new direction for vision restoration. Hussey is now a molecular and cell biologist at CiRC Biosciences, a cell therapy company in Chicago.

"The goal with using this organoid tech is to eventually make an almost made-to-order population of photoreceptors. A big avenue of potential is cell replacement therapy to introduce healthy cells that can reintegrate into the eye and potentially restore that lost vision," said Hussey.

The idea is to introduce healthy cells that could integrate with existing retinal tissue and potentially replace functions lost to disease. Achieving that goal would require researchers to demonstrate that transplanted cells can survive, connect properly with the eye's existing circuitry, and function safely.

Hussey emphasized that the technology remains far from routine clinical use, with extensive development and testing still necessary.

"These are very long-term experiments, and of course we'd need to do optimizations for safety and efficacy studies prior to moving into the clinic. But it's a viable journey."

For now, the discovery provides something fundamental: a clearer explanation of how the human eye develops its remarkable ability to see fine details. By revealing how vitamin A signaling and thyroid hormones help shape the retina, scientists have taken another step toward understanding vision at its earliest stages and potentially finding ways to restore it when disease strikes.

Materials provided by Johns Hopkins University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#692. Bayern Munich's Kenya friendly highlights Africa's growing pull for global sport

Bayern Munich are to open Nairobi's new Raila Odinga International Stadium against Ajax as Kenya prepares for AFCON 2027. The match highlights Africa's growing sports ambitions — and questions over cost and legacy.

Bundesliga champions Bayern Munich are to travel to Nairobi, Kenya during the winter break to play a friendly that opens the newly finished Raila Odinga International Stadium in the capital city. The German side will face Ajax Amsterdam as the game acts as part of the country's preparations for the 2027 African Cup of Nations (AFCON), which will be held in Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania next summer.

"Bayern has millions of fantastic fans in Africa with whom we feel a close connection – it's a continent with a huge passion for football," Rouven Kasper, Bayern board member for marketing and sales, said in a club statement.

"We will be making a further contribution to raising the profile of the Bundesliga and are very much looking forward to this special event."

The news is just the latest venture into global sports investing in Africa. Earlier this month, Formula 1 announced it was returning to the continent after Rwanda secured the rights for a deal from the early 2030s onwards. In September, World Athletics revealed Nairobi would host the World Championships in 2029. It will be the first time the event has been held in Africa.

Simon Chadwick, a business management and program director at the African School of Economics, believes that over the last two decades the professionalization and industrialization of sports has begun to emerge in Africa.

"Countries like Rwanda, Kenya, Morocco and obviously, South Africa, if we go back to the last decade of the previous century, have increasingly begun to deploy sport as a policy instrument," Chadwick told DW, adding Senegal and Egypt to the list.

"There are these image and reputational benefits which very often are bundled up as soft power. It's about attractiveness and appeal and engagement," said Chadwick.

"It's almost like a kind of professionalization, industrialization and politicization of sport that we're seeing elsewhere in the world has now arrived in Africa. We are seeing a much greater sense of kind of self-determination within Africa to do this," he added.

"This is not just about sport. It is also about diplomacy and bilateral trade, but also about the broader economic and industrial context within which sport sits."

For Kenya specifically, the building of the stadium is in line with the housing and sports infrastructural development that has been so heavily promoted under President William Ruto. Hosting this game is a symbol of the development currently happening in Nairobi.

"The bigger picture is that Nairobi now is positioning itself as a as an alternative sports venue," Richard Wanjohi, Editorial and Research Lead at the African Sports and Creative Institute (ASCI), told DW.

"I think we have seen what Kigali has done over the last number of years. For us to then come back into this conversation as a major city that can host such an event, it's huge. A few weeks later, we'll have the rugby sevens series again and then ultimately, the Africa Cup of Nations in July."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Chadwick believes that unlike Rwanda, Kenya's relative stability and pre-existing tourist industry allows for a more natural development of sports investment.

"This is not Kenya trying to build a tourism industry through an engagement in sport. I think it's an extension of what Kenya has been doing for a number of years through sport."

Combined with being a multi-sport country - athletics, rugby, football, volleyball – Wanjohi believes Kenya is ready to make the most of that performance on the field or track.

"It's about time that we also host the world and show them that we can do this from a hosting perspective, but also from developing infrastructure that is ready to host such sports events," Wanjohi said.

"It's beyond just saying that we have the talent that is already in the sport, but it's saying that we have the infrastructure, we have the skills, we have the capability to host this as any other African, if not global nation."

However, Ruto's government has been criticized over taxation, unemployment and its handling of dissent. Given that this stadium cost approximately €375 million ($418 million), it is perhaps no surprise that questions are being asked about the decision to invest in major sports infrastructure.

"People are asking, we are a struggling economy. There are a lot of other issues that could be addressed, like the education sector, health and all that. How did we get that money and be able to make that provision? Also interestingly, is that there's an appearance fee that is going to be paid to both Bayern and Ajax," said Wanjohi, who added there was also some frustration that the opening game was not given to local teams or even the national side.

Ultimately, the timing of this also matters. While many sports fans in the country are excited, others are critical.

"The government knows that this is almost like a campaign tool. We have an election coming up in August next year so the government or the president of the day obviously wants to use as much leverage of such an event to milk it for all it's worth," Wanjohi added.

"So the two different schools of thought are: It's a good thing to have, but at what cost are we doing it at and is it in the public interest as well?"

The proof will be in what the legacy of events like Bayern Munich's friendly in Nairobi brings Kenyan football. The feeling in late 2026 though, is largely optimistic.

"I guess the acid test is that many African nations carry with them the baggage from the past that this is just trophy asset investment that is ultimately going to create white, white elephant infrastructure," Chadwick said.

"But having spoken to people in Kenyan sport, in the industry itself, it seems to me that there is a genuine appetite for sports to become a genuine and legitimate driver of economic activity."

Janek Speight contributed reporting for this article.

#691. Hubble reveals a stunning twist in how the universe emerged from darkness

A surprising discovery made with NASA's Hubble Space Telescope is challenging a leading explanation for how the early universe emerged from darkness. The findings suggest that powerful explosions from dying stars may have actually interfered with a process scientists once believed they helped drive.

An international research team, including astronomers from the University of Michigan, found that powerful winds produced by exploding stars can prevent ultraviolet radiation from escaping galaxies. This is the opposite of what a widely accepted theory had predicted, and it could change how scientists understand one of the most important transformations in cosmic history.

The discovery, published in Nature Astronomy, offers new clues about how the universe became transparent to ultraviolet light roughly 13 billion years ago.

How the Early Universe Emerged From Its Cosmic Fog

During the first billion years after the Big Bang, vast amounts of neutral hydrogen filled the space between galaxies. This hydrogen formed a kind of cosmic fog that absorbed ultraviolet radiation, preventing that light from traveling freely across the universe.

That changed during a period known as reionization, which began approximately 13 billion years ago. Intense radiation from early galaxies gradually transformed the hydrogen by stripping electrons from its atoms, leaving behind positively charged protons and free electrons.

As more hydrogen became ionized, ultraviolet light could travel much farther through intergalactic space. This transformation helped establish the relatively transparent universe that astronomers observe today.

"Eventually, when it ionized the majority of hydrogen filling intergalactic space, that was the end of reionization and we see the universe today," said Cody Carr, a postdoctoral researcher in the University of Michigan's Department of Astronomy. "We call reionization the last major phase transition of the universe."

Despite its enormous importance, astronomers still do not fully understand which objects supplied the radiation responsible for reionization or how enough of that radiation managed to escape from early galaxies.

"We don't know exactly what objects caused reionization or how it evolved," said Carr, who conducted and led the research while working as a postdoctoral scholar at Zhejiang University in China, before joining the University of Michigan. "We know that it took place, but we don't have complete answers to those questions."

Hubble Challenges a Leading Theory About Exploding Stars

For years, one prominent explanation centered on supernovae, the powerful explosions that occur when certain stars reach the ends of their lives. These explosions can generate enormous winds that sweep through galaxies, pushing gas and other material outward.

Scientists proposed that these winds cleared pathways through the gas surrounding young stars, allowing ultraviolet radiation to escape into the space between galaxies. Once outside, that radiation could help break apart the neutral hydrogen responsible for the universe's ancient fog.

However, new observations from Hubble suggest that this explanation may have the process backward.

Rather than opening routes for radiation to escape, the researchers found that stronger galactic winds were associated with less escaping ionizing radiation. The observations indicate that the winds generated by supernovae can actually make it harder for the radiation to leave a galaxy.

"Basically, how these galaxies were leaking ionizing radiation isn't what we thought," Carr said.

The results lend support to a different possibility. Radiation from young, massive stars may escape their galaxies before those stars explode as supernovae and generate large winds that reshape the surrounding environment.

"Our observations show that these photons are escaping before galactic winds form," Carr said.

Photons are individual packets of light energy. In this case, the researchers are interested in ultraviolet photons energetic enough to ionize hydrogen, making them essential to understanding how the early universe became transparent.

What Hubble Discovered in Nearby Starburst Galaxies

To investigate how radiation escapes, the international team used the Hubble Space Telescope to examine nearby starburst galaxies. These are galaxies experiencing exceptionally intense periods of star formation, making them useful modern examples of the kinds of galaxies believed to have contributed to reionization.

Hubble, a NASA mission launched with contributions from the European Space Agency, allowed researchers to study the light coming from these galaxies in detail.

The team examined their spectra, which reveal how much light is present at different wavelengths. By studying the patterns in those spectra, astronomers can learn about the gas surrounding stars and determine how quickly it is moving.

Gas absorbs particular wavelengths of light, creating recognizable dips in a galaxy's spectrum. The locations and shapes of these dips provide clues about the speed and movement of galactic winds.

When the researchers compared wind speeds with the amount of ionizing radiation escaping from each galaxy, they uncovered a surprising relationship. Galaxies with the fastest winds allowed the smallest fraction of ionizing radiation to escape.

That result directly challenges the expectation that stronger winds should clear away more gas and make it easier for radiation to reach intergalactic space.

"It appears that energy input from supernovae has stirred up the surroundings and increased, rather than decreased, the coverage of neutral gas and dust that suppresses ionizing radiation escape," said Stephan McCandliss, a senior author of the study and director of the Center for Astrophysical Sciences at Johns Hopkins University.

In other words, instead of clearing a path for ultraviolet light, energy from exploding stars appears to redistribute gas and dust in ways that can block more of it.

Young Stars May Hold the Key to Cosmic Reionization

Although large galactic winds appear to suppress escaping radiation, smaller winds and other activity around young stars could still help create openings in the surrounding gas.

These processes may occur before the first supernova explosions, giving radiation a chance to escape while conditions are more favorable.

The findings suggest that astronomers may need to pay greater attention to what happens during the earliest stages of star formation, rather than focusing primarily on the effects of exploding stars.

Carr and his colleagues are seeking additional observing time with Hubble to examine more galaxies and investigate whether the same patterns appear elsewhere. More observations could help establish how important the activity of young stars is in allowing ionizing radiation to escape.

The results also have implications for computer simulations of the early universe. These simulations attempt to recreate how galaxies formed, how gas moved through them, and how radiation eventually transformed the hydrogen filling intergalactic space.

"Supernovae play a central role in cosmological hydrodynamic simulations that explain how ionizing radiation escapes from galaxies," said Renyue Cen, a senior author of the study and professor and director of the Center for Cosmology and Computational Astrophysics at Zhejiang University. "Our findings highlight the need to examine how radiation and winds from young stars shape the surrounding gas before the first supernovae explode."

By accounting more accurately for these early interactions between stars, radiation, and gas, researchers may be able to build better models of how reionization unfolded.

The discovery does not yet settle the question of what caused the universe's last major phase transition. However, it provides an important new clue, suggesting that the radiation that helped lift the universe's ancient fog may have escaped galaxies before powerful stellar explosions began to alter their surroundings.

International Research Collaboration and Funding

The research brought together nearly 30 scientists from more than a dozen institutions around the world. Sally Oey, a professor of astronomy at the University of Michigan, also contributed to the study.

The project received additional financial support from Zhejiang University, the Zhejiang Provincial Top-Level Research Support Program, the National Natural Science Foundation of China, the Ministry of Science, Innovation and Universities in Spain, the European Regional Development Fund, and the European Union's Horizon 2020 Research and Innovation Program.

The research was also supported in part by federal funding from NASA and the U.S. National Science Foundation. Additional support for the Hubble Space Telescope observations came through a grant administered by the Space Telescope Science Institute.

Materials provided by University of Michigan. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

On Episode 234 of This Week In Space, Tariq Malik and Mike Wall are joined by Than Putzig of the Planetary Science Institute about a NASA-backed payload bound for the Marius Hills Pit on the moon.

In our ongoing quest to develop a moon base, could we possibly utilize the area beneath the surface of the moon in order to make the moon habitable? Could Marius Hills Pit, a roughly 50-meter-wide opening that may lead into a lunar lava tube, become the Moon's first living habitat for humans?

Putzig explains how geophysical instruments on a rover could detect hidden voids beneath the surface and measure the size of these lava tubes. We also ask Than how these lava tubes form, what a follow-up robotic explorer could reveal, and how this research fits alongside NASA’s Artemis plans for a south polar moon base. Join us!
